t: Number of Unique Good Subsequences - Linear DP on the Last Character
o: Among all $2^n - 1$ subsequences of the binary string, we count the DISTINCT ones that are good: non-empty and free of leading zeros, with the single character "0" allowed. In "001" only "0" and "1" qualify (anything longer starting with those zeros has a leading zero), so the answer is 2; in "11" the unique good ones are "1" and "11". Duplicates must collapse - three physical copies of "0" count once. Since the string can be up to 100000 characters, anything enumerating subsequences is hopeless and a linear scan tracking two counters plus a zero-flag is the intended solution.
k: Partitioning unique good subsequences by their last character makes extension safe: appending a fixed character to disjoint suffix classes keeps results distinct.
The bare string "0" can never be extended into a good subsequence, so it is tracked by a boolean flag instead of a counter.
"Only extend using the newest occurrence" is how classic distinct-subsequence DP deduplicates; the two-counter recurrence encodes this implicitly.
w: Give the two-counter DP; keep enumeration only for testing small cases. Pitfalls: forgetting the standalone "0" whenever the string contains any zero (the answer comes out one short), adding 1 unconditionally for it, and overflowing fixed-width integers in C++ or Java before the modulo (use 64-bit intermediates). Edge cases to test: all zeros (answer 1), all ones (answer grows like all distinct strings of ones), and a single character. Follow-ups: generalize beyond binary alphabets using per-character last-occurrence DP, or count distinct good subsequences of each length.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate All Subsequences Into a Set
a.i: Every non-empty subset of positions defines a subsequence string; filter those with a leading zero (keeping bare "0"), insert survivors into a hash set, and return its size. This is the definitional baseline: it is trivially correct and useful for validating the fast solution on small inputs, but it materializes exponentially many strings.
s: Iterate all bitmasks from 1 to $2^n - 1$, each encoding a non-empty position subset.
Build the subsequence string for the current mask.
Keep it only if it starts with "1" or equals "0".
Insert kept strings into a set and return the set size modulo $10^9 + 7$.
a.t: O(2^n * n) - every mask builds a length-n string, hopeless at n = 100000 but fine for tiny tests
a.sp: O(2^n * n) - the set may hold exponentially many distinct strings

a.n: Approach 2: Linear DP Tracking Counts by Last Character
a.i: Maintain end1 and end0: the number of unique good subsequences that start with "1" and end in "1" or "0" respectively. When a new "1" arrives, the fresh unique strings ending here are every previous string extended by this "1" plus bare "1" - three disjoint suffix classes (...11, ...01, and "1"), so uniqueness is preserved and end1 becomes end1 + end0 + 1. A new "0" similarly sets end0 = end0 + end1; leading-zero strings are never good, so the standalone "0" is remembered only through a boolean flag rather than being extendable.
s: Initialize end1 = end0 = 0 and hasZero = false.
On reading "1", update end1 = end1 + end0 + 1 modulo $10^9 + 7$.
On reading "0", update end0 = end0 + end1 and set hasZero = true.
Return end0 + end1 + (1 if hasZero else 0) modulo $10^9 + 7$.
a.t: O(n) - a single scan with O(1) modular work per character
a.sp: O(1) - two counters and a flag
